title: How to Do Performance Reviews
author: Ojstersek, Gregor
summary: Gregor Ojstersek shares a comprehensive guide to running effective performance reviews, drawn from managing engineering teams at scale. The article argues that performance reviews fail most commonly because they are treated as annual compliance events rather than ongoing dialogues with a formal checkpoint. Ojstersek outlines his personal system: establishing clear, written performance expectations at the start of each period; maintaining a continuous record of wins and development areas throughout the year; and structuring the review conversation to be genuinely two-way, with the team member's self-assessment preceding the leader's. He emphasizes that the goal of a performance review is not to deliver a verdict but to align on a shared picture of performance and create a concrete development plan. The piece also addresses calibration across a team and the communication challenge of delivering difficult feedback without ambiguity.
points: Performance reviews fail when they're compliance events, not ongoing dialogues: the formal review should consolidate a year of continuous feedback, not introduce new information.
Start with clear, written expectations: the conditions for a meaningful review are set at the beginning of the period, not during the review itself.
Lead with the team member's self-assessment: hearing their perspective first prevents the review from becoming a verdict and surfaces gaps in understanding before the leader's assessment.
Calibration across a team requires explicit conversation: ratings that mean different things to different managers are useless; calibration sessions force the consistency that makes reviews credible.
Development plans must be specific and time-bound: a review that ends with vague aspirations has failed -- concrete next steps with clear owners and timelines are required.
quotes: Full guide on how to set up successful performance reviews based on my personal experience and what has worked best for me and my teams.
The biggest mistake leaders make with performance reviews is treating them as the beginning of a conversation that should have been ongoing all year.
Before you write your assessment, ask the team member to write theirs. You will learn more from what they emphasize and what they omit than from anything else in the process.

Calibration is not about making everyone the same. It's about ensuring that 'meets expectations' means the same thing across your whole team -- and that people are not rated by how much their manager likes them.
A development plan that doesn't have a deadline and an owner is a wish list. The review isn't over until the plan is concrete enough to be held accountable.
